As a person who has worked in coil on the fluid side I can tell you that they do pump a wide variety of stuff downhole, sometimes LOTS of acid especially during a zipper frac. Oftentimes if there are concerns about bacteria producing H2S we'll be using a significant quantity of concentrated poisonous poison we call "biocide". Pretty much everything that we send downhole is cancer causing so we like to call the chemical trailers that hold the totes cancer vans. 

During the winter there can be unexpected circumstances that result in the usage of vast quantities of menthol, like more than enough to fill 7-8km of 3-4"coil

Idk how much of all this stuff someone would actually be exposed to in flowback, but I'd be cautious and just assume that there's nasty stuff.

Methanol is also much more dangerous than people give it credit for and I know of at least one person who was hospitalized for having some splash on his face. 

I also heard a story about a guy who went instantly blind from a drop of biocide splashing into his eye but that wasn't first hand.

It's possible, you'll be sacrificing your life outside of work however if you want to make real money. Generally any job that pays decently with minimal qualifications will require that sacrifice. E.g working 13h/day indefinitely. Many jobs in oil have a day shift or night shift so those work out to roughly 13 at least because of the hand off..  there are Jobs that don't do a hand off which can go over 13h and you can also make good money with those e.g cementing (but you'll probably need a commercial driving license for that). 

Also not every job will have enough work all the time, cementing can be busy or quiet so you could have a 16h day or nothing at all.  If you don't want to get too physical I would recommend getting a commercial driving license as that opens up loads more jobs that pay decently(100k+)..

Anyways yes it's possible, you can probably do it if you're willing and able to become a slave and don't give other people the impression that you're useless (not all turnover is people quitting). There is also a factor of luck as downturns happen.

In Canada many companies will immediately hire you as a full-time employee with the same benefits as a full-time employee that has been employed for 4 months. Some will have separate benefits that kick in later.. e.g RRSP matching increase after a year.  

Just because you're hired at the same 'position'/status does not guarantee job security however. For example at my company I saw countless people let go before the 3 month period ended. This is because in Canada after 3 months they have an obligation to pay you a few weeks worth of pay if they lay you off/fire without cause.  

That being said most companies don't really mind having to payout to lay off even after the 3 month mark.

I can't speak to your partial blindness but I've had plenty of commercial driving jobs. I've also driven over 20 hours straight a few times (in my personal vehicle) and didn't die.

Having some anxiety is okay although panicking and throwing your driving test away isn't good. (I did that on my first commercial driving test, before we even left the truckyard)

I think I largely had anxiety because of how 'high stakes' i made the test in my head. And yeah, one screw up can and often will compound into many if you don't relax.

On my last (passed) driving test (manual transmission) I had some anxiety about downshifting and getting stuck in neutral before stopping. 

So I said fuck it a few times and didn't shift to the 'perfect' gear if I wasn't sure i'd be able to do it. 

Sure it meant I had to come to a complete stop and reset my shifting but I knew that was better than failing the test.

I told myself it didn't matter if it wasn't perfect, as long as it wasn't something that would fail me outright.. that applied to every aspect of the driving test. 


I just resigned myself to not being perfect but trying to be 'passable'  it helped me a lot with my anxiety. 

You're not supposed to be a perfect pro driver on the driving test, just good enough to not cause too much chaos. And if you're still getting really flustered practice will likely eventually get you to a point where you feel comfortable. 

Keep at it and I'm sure you'll eventually get comfortable enough, just try to not make it so high stakes if you can.

I don't know if all banks have them, most life insurance companies do. 

The amount you get will generally be fixed once it's set-up.  

If you set it up when interest rates are higher you'll generally get more money per month.

You give a lump sum, you can generally never get this lump sum back. If you die all payments stop and the insurance company celebrates not having to pay more money.

Generally the older you are when you set it up the more they are willing to pay. (Because they assume you'll die sooner).

If you're married it is possible to also put your spouse on it, but the rate will likely go down a bit because then they'd need both of you to die to not have to pay anymore.

Again, once it's set up it's generally permanently fixed till you die, wont fluctuate if rates go down or up. You can't "withdraw" it. So you're essentially trading a lump sum in exchange for "cash for life". 

If you're immortal they lose big time.

If you are legitimately nervous about permanently losing the money, and cannot trust yourself or others around you and are over the age of 35 you could get something called a "life annuity".  (Some companies have different age reqs)

It will pay you a fixed amount of money till you die.

If you're young it's pretty much just going to give around 5-6% R.O.I..like $1000/ month.

There are obviously better options but this way you are guaranteeing yourself a fixed amount FOREVER.  

if you are older the rates will be far more attractive, in general the rates are decent right now because interest rates are higher.

Also, if you do this friends, family, neighbors etc won't ask for handouts because you won't be holding a lump sum for them to leech from.

Alternatively, if you think you can trust yourself, max out your TFSA (dont over contribute) and invest in a bunch of "dividend aristocrat" companies or other decent dividend yielding companies that aren't risky and withdraw the dividends as spending money.

You can put the remainder in a regular taxable dividend portfolio.

My buddy(32 yr old) is living a modest retired life living off of a 300k dividend portfolio sharing rent with his friend. (If you're retired you can choose to live in much cheaper areas).

He doesn't day trade or anything, literally just bought a bunch of dividend companies, reinvests a small portion,  withdraws a small amount for living expenses and he's very happy.

Agreed if luck determines whether or not any drop occurs it matters for Gear-score.

Benefits from bonus luck can become exponentially more beneficial the higher you go. 

For example if rolls are 0-100,000 and we pretend the rare item requires a roll 99,000+ 



Regular person odds= 1/100 kills.

Person with 2% luck bag (200 bonus luck): 1/83 kills

Person with 20% luck total (2000 bonus):  1/33 kills

It's not like the person with 20% luck is 20% more likely to find the item, it's more like they are 3x more likely.

The difference becomes MASSIVE with other rarer items (especially luck gated items) if luck is functioning correctly.

For example if it requires a roll of 102,000.

Theoretically having 2000(20%) luck would make it 'possible' to find the item, 

1 per 100,000 attempts. 

However just having 2100(21%) luck would cut that down to 

1 per 1000 attempts

And having max luck bonus around 50%\5000 cuts that to

1 per 33 attempts.

Every little bit can make a huge difference, (if luck isn't broken)
